body_markdown:
Almost every motorbike rental in Hanoi ends the same way: the shop hands back a deposit. What separates a smooth return from a disputed one is not the size of the deposit but the terms agreed before the keys changed hands. Who holds the money or the passport? What reduces the refund: damage, late return, fuel level, traffic tickets? When and how is the deposit returned? This guide walks through how deposits work in Hanoi's rental market, what a reasonable range looks like, and which terms to fix in writing before riding off. For the physical condition checks that protect your deposit, the [rental checklist for Hanoi](/en/checklist/) is the companion piece.

## What deposits look like in practice

Hanoi shops commonly ask for two things at handover: identification and a deposit. A large Hanoi rental operator states its terms openly: renters provide an ID document, and a deposit ranging from 2,000,000 to 5,000,000 VND, roughly 80 to 200 US dollars ([Rent Bike Hanoi](https://rentbikehanoi.com/)). Other operators scale the deposit by bike type and some go further: one rental company that also handles larger displacement bikes keeps the renter's passport for the whole rental period and returns it at the drop-off location (Rental Motorbike Vietnam, [rental terms](https://rentalmotorbikevietnam.com/)).

Both practices are routine in Vietnam, but they carry different risks. A cash deposit is a fixed, documented amount that either comes back or does not. A passport is not a deposit; it is your primary identity document abroad, and handing it over means the shop, not you, controls your mobility for the entire rental. Many foreign embassies and travel advisories recommend keeping your passport in your own possession while abroad. Where a shop insists on holding a passport, a reasonable compromise to negotiate is a cash deposit instead.

## What actually reduces a refund

Deposit disputes almost never come from the deposit itself; they come from the terms around it. Four categories account for nearly all deductions. First, damage: scratches, broken mirrors, bent levers, damaged panels. The disagreement is rarely whether damage exists, but whether it existed before your rental. Second, late return: hourly or daily surcharges, sometimes steeper than the daily rate itself. Third, fuel: the tank level at handover versus the level at return. Fourth, penalties: if the bike accumulates traffic fines while in your possession, for example from traffic cameras, the registered owner must identify the rider under Article 47 of [Decree 168/2024/NĐ-CP](https://xaydungchinhsach.chinhphu.vn/toan-van-nghi-dinh-168-2024-nd-cp-quy-dinh-xu-phat-vi-pham-hanh-chinh-ve-trat-tu-atgt-duong-bo-119241231164556785.htm), as the Ministry of Public Security explains in its [guidance on self-drive rentals](https://mps.gov.vn/hoi-dap/chi-tiet-cau-hoi/7511a592-d684-4380-978a-26ebfc4adff4), so the shop may expect you to settle them before releasing the deposit.

The pattern behind all four is documentation asymmetry. If nobody photographed the bike's condition at handover, the memory of that state belongs to whoever is holding the deposit. That asymmetry is avoidable: photograph every panel, wheel, mirror and lever at pickup, ask the shop to do the same jointly, and keep the photos timestamped on your own phone. The [rental checklist](/en/checklist/) builds this step into the handover sequence precisely because it is the single strongest protection for your deposit.

## Cash, cards, and the mechanics of the refund

In Hanoi, deposits are overwhelmingly cash transactions, and that shapes the refund mechanics. Cash in means cash out: you should expect the refund at the moment the bike passes inspection at return, not by bank transfer days later. If a shop proposes returning a cash deposit "later" or by transfer, treat that as a warning sign and prefer a shop that refunds on the spot.

Cards change the logic in one important way. If a shop takes a card imprint or a pre-authorization, the "refund" is a release of a hold, which depends on your bank and can take days to appear. Pre-authorizations are rare in Vietnamese rental shops but appear occasionally with higher-value bikes. Before agreeing to a card hold, ask two questions: when the hold will be released, and whether the release happens at the shop or at your bank. The answers determine how quickly the money is usable again.

## Deposit terms worth fixing in writing

Five terms deserve a written record, even in a short message thread with the shop. One: the exact deposit amount and its currency. Two: what it covers, and specifically whether it covers damage only or also fuel, lateness, and traffic tickets. Three: the return conditions, meaning the time, place, and inspection procedure. Four: the refund method and timing, ideally "cash on the spot after inspection". Five: the damage baseline, meaning a shared set of photos or a signed condition note. A shop that answers these five questions in a chat message has, in effect, written you a mini-contract. A shop that refuses to answer any of them is telling you something about the return experience.

This matters more for long rentals. At monthly rates of 900,000–2,000,000 VND ([Rent Bike Hanoi](https://rentbikehanoi.com/)), a 2,000,000–5,000,000 VND deposit can exceed the rental fee itself, and the incentive to document the bike's condition carefully grows with every week you keep it. For multi-week rentals, do the handover inspection with the same seriousness as a purchase.

## Passport holds: how to evaluate the trade

Because passport holds are a documented practice at some Hanoi operators (Rental Motorbike Vietnam, [FAQ](https://rentalmotorbikevietnam.com/)), the question is not whether it happens, but how to respond when it does. Three factors matter. First, the length of the rental: a one-day hold on a small bike is a different risk from a two-week hold on a high-value bike. Second, what you receive in exchange: a passport held against a written agreement with a named shop address is different from a passport held against nothing. Third, your alternatives: if you hold a second photo ID, some shops accept it alongside a cash deposit instead.

If you do hand over your passport, mitigate the exposure: carry a photocopy and a phone photo of the ID page, know your embassy's replacement procedure, and keep the shop's written rental agreement that names you as the renter. If the shop cannot produce a written agreement, that fact weighs more heavily than any deposit discount.

## Questions to ask before handing anything over

First: what is the deposit amount, and can it be paid in cash instead of leaving my passport? Second: what exactly can be deducted from it, and how is the bike's condition documented at pickup? Third: when and how is the refund paid after return? Combined with the price tiers of daily, weekly and monthly rentals on the [English homepage](/en/), these three answers give you the complete financial picture of the rental. The deposit is the one part of the transaction that ends the trip, and it deserves the same care as the ride itself. For the step-by-step condition documentation that protects the refund, start with the [rental checklist](/en/checklist/).
